beats.say: Priya and Rohan are given 540 rupees to divide in the ratio 4 to 5, and Rohan gets the larger share. He spends 80 rupees and gives the rest to his mother. How much does she get?
Think of the ratio as equal boxes: 4 parts for Priya and 5 parts for Rohan.
Before sharing anything, count. How many equal parts altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 4 and 5 make 9 parts.

beats.say: Add the ratio numbers: 4 plus 5 makes 9. All 540 rupees sit in those 9 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 540 divided by 9 is 60, so each part is 60 rupees. Careful: we divide by all 9 parts, not by one of the ratio numbers on its own.
Rohan gets the larger share, so he has the 5 parts. Which sum gives that share?

ask.ifNot: Rohan gets the larger share, so he has the 5 parts. One part is 60 rupees, so we want 5 lots of 60.

beats.say: 5 times 60 is 300. So Rohan gets 300 rupees.
Rohan spends 80 rupees on firecrackers, so we take 80 away from his 300. That leaves 220 for his mother.
So Rohan gives his mother 220 rupees.
Check the sharing. Priya has 4 parts, and 4 times 60 is 240. 240 plus 300 is 540, the whole amount, so the shares are right.
So every time: total parts first, then the size of one part, then the share. And read the last line of the story to see what is still left to do.
Rohit and Virat scored 180 runs together, in the ratio 5 to 4. In the next match Rohit scored twice as many as in the first. We want Rohit's runs in the second match.
Read the ratio as parts: 5 parts for Rohit and 4 parts for Virat, and every part is the same size. Look at the boxes.
First job: how many equal parts are there in all?

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 5 and 4 make 9 parts.

beats.say: Add the ratio numbers: 5 plus 4 makes 9. All 180 runs sit in those 9 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 180 divided by 9 is 20, so each part is 20 runs. Careful: we divide by all 9 parts, not by one of the ratio numbers on its own.
Rohit has 5 parts. Which sum gives that share?

ask.ifNot: Rohit has 5 parts. One part is 20 runs, so we want 5 lots of 20.

beats.say: 5 times 20 is 100. So Rohit scored 100 runs in the first match.
In the second match he scored twice as many. Twice means 2 times, and 2 times 100 is 200.
So Rohit scored 200 runs in the second match. Stopping at 100 is the trap: that was only the first match.
Check the sharing. Virat has 4 parts, and 4 times 20 is 80. 100 plus 80 is 180, the whole amount, so the shares are right.
So the plan for sharing in a ratio: add the ratio numbers to count the parts, divide the total to find one part, then multiply by the parts you need.
Priya and Rohan share 1,800 rupees in the ratio 2 to 3. Priya then spends her share on diyas and candles in the ratio 3 to 5. We want the money she spends on candles.
Think of the ratio as equal boxes: 2 parts for Priya and 3 parts for Rohan.
First job: how many equal parts are there in all?

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 2 and 3 make 5 parts.

beats.say: Add the ratio numbers: 2 plus 3 makes 5. All 1,800 rupees sit in those 5 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 1,800 divided by 5 is 360, so each part is 360 rupees. The classic slip is to divide by just one ratio number, but the total belongs to all 5 parts.
Priya has 2 parts, and each part is 360 rupees. 2 times 360 is 720, so Priya gets 720 rupees.
Now a second sharing begins. This time the amount being shared is Priya's 720 rupees, not the 1,800. Her ratio is 3 to 5, so how many parts this time?

ask.ifNot: This is a new ratio, 3 to 5, for diyas and candles. 3 parts and 5 parts make 8 parts.

beats.say: 3 plus 5 is 8. 720 divided by 8 is 90, so each of these new parts is 90 rupees.
Candles are the second number in that ratio, so they take 5 parts. 5 times 90 is 450.
So Priya spends 450 rupees on candles.
Check: diyas take 3 parts, and 3 times 90 is 270. 270 plus 450 is 720, exactly Priya's share.
So with two ratios, one after the other, do the same three moves twice: count the parts, find one part, multiply. Just be sure the second time you share the right amount.
Riya and Sana collected 770 rupees in the ratio 4 to 7. Sana spends her whole share on notebooks that cost 14 rupees each. How many notebooks can she buy?
Read the ratio as parts: 4 parts for Riya and 7 parts for Sana, and every part is the same size. Look at the boxes.
First job: how many equal parts are there in all?

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 4 and 7 make 11 parts.

beats.say: Add the ratio numbers: 4 plus 7 makes 11. All 770 rupees sit in those 11 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 770 divided by 11 is 70, so each part is 70 rupees. The classic slip is to divide by just one ratio number, but the total belongs to all 11 parts.
Sana has 7 parts, and each part is 70 rupees. 7 times 70 is 490, so Sana gets 490 rupees.
Each notebook costs 14 rupees. How do we find how many notebooks 490 rupees will buy?

ask.ifNot: We want to know how many 14s fit into 490. Counting how many times one number fits into another is division.

beats.say: 14 times 30 is 420, and 14 times 5 is 70. Together that makes 490, so 14 goes into 490 exactly 35 times.
So Sana can buy 35 notebooks.
Check the sharing. Riya has 4 parts, and 4 times 70 is 280. 280 plus 490 is 770, the whole amount, so the shares are right.
So remember three moves: count the parts, find one part, multiply for the share. Then do whatever else the story asks.

Think of the ratio as equal boxes: 3 parts for the morning and 5 parts for the evening.
First job: how many equal parts are there in all?

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 3 and 5 make 8 parts.

beats.say: Add the ratio numbers: 3 plus 5 makes 8. All 72 samosas sit in those 8 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 72 divided by 8 is 9, so each part is 9 samosas. The classic slip is to divide by just one ratio number, but the total belongs to all 8 parts.
The morning is the first number, so it has 3 parts. Which sum gives that share?

ask.ifNot: The morning is the first number, so it has 3 parts. One part is 9 samosas, so we want 3 lots of 9.

beats.say: 3 times 9 is 27. So Ananya sold 27 samosas in the morning.
Bhavna sold twice as many as that. Twice means 2 times, and 2 times 27 is 54.
So Bhavna sold 54 samosas. Notice it is twice Ananya's morning number, not twice her whole 72.
Check the sharing. The evening has 5 parts, and 5 times 9 is 45. 27 plus 45 is 72, the whole amount, so the shares are right.
So the plan for sharing in a ratio: add the ratio numbers to count the parts, divide the total to find one part, then multiply by the parts you need.

Rohit is named first, so he has the first number, 5 parts. Which sum gives that share?

ask.ifNot: Rohit is named first, so he has the first number, 5 parts. One part is 14 runs, so we want 5 lots of 14.

beats.say: 5 times 14 is 70. So Rohit gets 70 runs.
That is our answer: 70 runs for Rohit.
Check the sharing. Virat has 4 parts, and 4 times 14 is 56. 70 plus 56 is 126, the whole amount, so the shares are right.

Kabir, Priya and Zara split a profit of 450 rupees in the ratio 2 to 3 to 5. Kabir gives half of his share to charity. How much does he have left?
Read the ratio as parts: 2 parts for Kabir, 3 parts for Priya and 5 parts for Zara, and every part is the same size. Look at the boxes.
First job: how many equal parts are there in all?

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 2 and 3 and 5 make 10 parts.

beats.say: Add the ratio numbers: 2 plus 3 plus 5 makes 10. All 450 rupees sit in those 10 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 450 divided by 10 is 45, so each part is 45 rupees. The classic slip is to divide by just one ratio number, but the total belongs to all 10 parts.
Kabir has 2 parts. Which sum gives that share?

ask.ifNot: Kabir has 2 parts. One part is 45 rupees, so we want 2 lots of 45.

beats.say: 2 times 45 is 90. So Kabir gets 90 rupees.
Kabir donates half of his 90 rupees. 90 divided by 2 is 45, so he gives 45 away and keeps the other 45.
So Kabir has 45 rupees left. That is the size of one part, which makes sense: half of 2 parts is 1 part.
Check the sharing. Priya has 3 parts, and 3 times 45 is 135 and Zara has 5 parts, and 5 times 45 is 225. 90 plus 135 plus 225 is 450, the whole amount, so the shares are right.
So the plan for sharing in a ratio: add the ratio numbers to count the parts, divide the total to find one part, then multiply by the parts you need.
Arjun, Bharat and Chetan scored 225 runs in the ratio 3 to 5 to 7. The coach gives 10 rupees for every run. How much more money does Chetan get than Arjun?
Read the ratio as parts: 3 parts for Arjun, 5 parts for Bharat and 7 parts for Chetan, and every part is the same size. Look at the boxes.
First job: how many equal parts are there in all?

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 3 and 5 and 7 make 15 parts.

beats.say: Add the ratio numbers: 3 plus 5 plus 7 makes 15. All 225 runs sit in those 15 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 225 divided by 15 is 15, so each part is 15 runs. The classic slip is to divide by just one ratio number, but the total belongs to all 15 parts.
Arjun has 3 parts: 3 times 15 is 45. Chetan has 7 parts: 7 times 15 is 105.
We only need Chetan and Arjun. How many more runs did Chetan score than Arjun?

ask.ifNot: How many more asks for the gap between Chetan's 105 and Arjun's 45. To find a gap, take the smaller from the bigger.

beats.say: 105 minus 45 is 60. Chetan scored 60 runs more.
Each run earns 10 rupees. So 60 extra runs earn 60 times 10, which is 600 rupees.
So Chetan receives 600 rupees more than Arjun.
Check it another way. Arjun earns 45 times 10, which is 450 rupees, and Chetan earns 105 times 10, which is 1,050. 1,050 minus 450 is 600 again.
So the plan: count the parts, find one part, multiply for each share. Then find the gap, and only at the end turn runs into rupees.
Priya and Rohan split 180 rupees in the ratio of their ages. Then Priya spends 45 rupees, and after that cousin Ankit gives them 50 rupees more, shared the same way. How much does Priya have now?

board.text: Then ₹50 more, shared the same way

beats.say: Priya is 12 years old and Rohan is 8. So the ratio of their ages, Priya to Rohan, is 12 to 8.
Those numbers can be made simpler. What is the biggest number that divides both 12 and 8 exactly?

ask.ifNot: 12 is 3 times 4, and 8 is 2 times 4. Nothing bigger goes into both.

beats.say: 12 divided by 4 is 3, and 8 divided by 4 is 2. So 12 to 8 is the same ratio as 3 to 2, just in smaller numbers.
A ratio of 3 to 2 means equal parts: 3 parts for Priya and 2 parts for Rohan. Here they are as boxes.
Before sharing anything, count. How many equal parts altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 3 and 2 make 5 parts.

beats.say: Add the ratio numbers: 3 plus 2 makes 5. All 180 rupees sit in those 5 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 180 divided by 5 is 36, so each part is 36 rupees. The classic slip is to divide by just one ratio number, but the total belongs to all 5 parts.
Priya has 3 parts, and each part is 36 rupees. 3 times 36 is 108, so Priya gets 108 rupees.
Next, Priya spends 45 rupees on sparklers. 108 minus 45 is 63.
Ankit's 50 rupees are shared the same way, into 5 parts. 50 divided by 5 is 10, and Priya's 3 parts make 3 times 10, which is 30.
Add that to what she had left: 63 plus 30 is 93.
So Priya has 93 rupees now. We followed her money in order: a share, a spend, then another share.
Check the sharing. Rohan has 2 parts, and 2 times 36 is 72. 108 plus 72 is 180, the whole amount, so the shares are right.
So the plan for sharing in a ratio: add the ratio numbers to count the parts, divide the total to find one part, then multiply by the parts you need.
Sneha and Tanvi bought 84 water balloons together, and they share them in the ratio of the money each one paid. We want Tanvi's balloons.
Sneha paid 35 rupees and Tanvi paid 49 rupees. So the ratio, Sneha to Tanvi, is 35 to 49.

Before sharing anything, count. How many equal parts altogether?

To find one part, we divide: 84 divided by 12 is 7, so each part is 7 balloons. Careful: we divide by all 12 parts, not by one of the ratio numbers on its own.
Tanvi has 7 parts, and each part is 7 balloons. 7 times 7 is 49, so Tanvi gets 49 balloons.
That is our answer. It is only a coincidence that Tanvi also paid 49 rupees: the money gave us the ratio, not the share.
Check the sharing. Sneha has 5 parts, and 5 times 7 is 35. 35 plus 49 is 84, the whole amount, so the shares are right.
So the plan for sharing in a ratio: add the ratio numbers to count the parts, divide the total to find one part, then multiply by the parts you need.

Karan gets the larger share, so he has the 5 parts, and each part is 60 rupees. 5 times 60 is 300, so Karan gets 300 rupees.
Now a second sharing begins. This time the amount being shared is Karan's 300 rupees, not the 540. His ratio is 2 to 3, so how many parts this time?

ask.ifNot: This is a new ratio, 2 to 3, for sparklers and rockets. 2 parts and 3 parts make 5 parts.

beats.say: 2 plus 3 is 5. 300 divided by 5 is 60, so each of these new parts is 60 rupees.
Rockets are the second number in that ratio, so they take 3 parts. 3 times 60 is 180.
So Karan spends 180 rupees on rockets.
Check: sparklers take 2 parts, and 2 times 60 is 120. 120 plus 180 is 300, exactly Karan's share.
So with two ratios, one after the other, do the same three moves twice: count the parts, find one part, multiply. Just be sure the second time you share the right amount.

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 3 and 4 make 7 parts.

beats.say: Add the ratio numbers: 3 plus 4 makes 7. All 84 runs sit in those 7 equal parts.

ask.ifNot: Sanjay has 4 parts. One part is 12 runs, so we want 4 lots of 12.

beats.say: 4 times 12 is 48. So Sanjay gets 48 runs.
That is our answer: 48 runs for Sanjay.
Check the sharing. Ravi has 3 parts, and 3 times 12 is 36. 36 plus 48 is 84, the whole amount, so the shares are right.

Coach Sharma shares 84 balls between Team Sixer and Team Boundary in the ratio 3 to 4. Later, 5 balls move from Team Boundary to Team Sixer. We want the new ratio.

board.text: Then 5 balls go from Boundary to Sixer

beats.say: Read the ratio as parts: 3 parts for Team Sixer and 4 parts for Team Boundary, and every part is the same size. Look at the boxes.
Before sharing anything, count. How many equal parts altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 3 and 4 make 7 parts.

beats.say: 3 plus 4 is 7. So the 84 balls are shared into 7 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 84 divided by 7 is 12, so each part is 12 balls. The classic slip is to divide by just one ratio number, but the total belongs to all 7 parts.
Team Sixer has 3 parts: 3 times 12 is 36. Team Boundary has 4 parts: 4 times 12 is 48.
Now 5 balls move from Team Boundary to Team Sixer. What happens to the two numbers?

ask.ifNot: The 5 balls leave Team Boundary, so Boundary loses 5. They arrive at Team Sixer, so Sixer gains 5. Both numbers change.

beats.say: 36 plus 5 is 41 for Team Sixer. 48 minus 5 is 43 for Team Boundary.
So the new ratio is 41 to 43. No number bigger than 1 divides both 41 and 43, so it cannot be made any simpler.
Check: no ball was lost, they only changed teams. 41 plus 43 is still 84.
So the plan: share in the ratio first to get real numbers, make the change the story describes to those numbers, then write the new ratio.
Arjun and Kabir scored 108 runs together, in the ratio 4 to 5. By how many runs did Kabir outscore Arjun?
Read the ratio as parts: 4 parts for Arjun and 5 parts for Kabir, and every part is the same size. Look at the boxes.
First job: how many equal parts are there in all?

beats.say: Add the ratio numbers: 4 plus 5 makes 9. All 108 runs sit in those 9 equal parts.

Arjun has 4 parts: 4 times 12 is 48. Kabir has 5 parts: 5 times 12 is 60.
The question asks by how many runs Kabir outscored Arjun. What do we do with 60 and 48?

ask.ifNot: How much more asks for the gap between the two shares. To find a gap, take the smaller from the bigger: 60 minus 48.

beats.say: 60 minus 48 is 12. That gap is what the question wants.
So Kabir outscored Arjun by 12 runs.
Check it another way. Kabir has just 1 part more than Arjun, and 1 part is 12. The same answer, so we can trust it.
So remember three moves: count the parts, find one part, multiply for the share. Then do whatever else the story asks.
Priya and Rohan buy a box of 90 sparklers and share them in the ratio of the money each one paid. How many more sparklers does Priya get than Rohan?
Priya paid 60 rupees and Rohan paid 30 rupees. So the ratio, Priya to Rohan, is 60 to 30.
Those numbers can be made simpler. What is the biggest number that divides both 60 and 30 exactly?

ask.ifNot: 60 is 2 times 30, and 30 goes into itself once. Nothing bigger goes into both.

beats.say: 60 divided by 30 is 2, and 30 divided by 30 is 1. So 60 to 30 is the same ratio as 2 to 1, just in smaller numbers.
A ratio of 2 to 1 means equal parts: 2 parts for Priya and 1 part for Rohan. Here they are as boxes.
Before sharing anything, count. How many equal parts altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 2 and 1 make 3 parts.

beats.say: 2 plus 1 is 3. So the 90 sparklers are shared into 3 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 90 divided by 3 is 30, so each part is 30 sparklers. Careful: we divide by all 3 parts, not by one of the ratio numbers on its own.
Priya has 2 parts: 2 times 30 is 60. Rohan has 1 part: 1 times 30 is 30.
The question asks how many more sparklers Priya gets than Rohan. That is the gap between the two shares, so we take the smaller from the bigger: 60 minus 30 is 30.
So Priya gets 30 more sparklers than Rohan.
Check it another way. Priya has just 1 part more than Rohan, and 1 part is 30. The same answer, so we can trust it.
So remember three moves: count the parts, find one part, multiply for the share. Then do whatever else the story asks.

Riya has 5 parts, and each part is 2 accessories. 5 times 2 is 10, so Riya gets 10 accessories.

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 5 and 4 make 9 parts.

beats.say: 5 plus 4 is 9. So the 360 rupees are shared into 9 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 360 divided by 9 is 40, so each part is 40 rupees. The classic slip is to divide by just one ratio number, but the total belongs to all 9 parts.
Ananya has 5 parts, and each part is 40 rupees. 5 times 40 is 200, so Ananya gets 200 rupees.
Each gift box costs 30 rupees, so count in 30s. 6 boxes cost 6 times 30, which is 180. 7 boxes would cost 210.
Ananya has 200 rupees. So how many boxes can she buy?

ask.ifNot: 7 boxes cost 210 rupees, and she only has 200, so 7 is too many. And a shop will not sell part of a box. 6 is the most she can buy.

beats.say: 6 boxes use up 180 rupees. 200 minus 180 leaves 20 rupees, which is not enough for another box.
So Ananya can buy 6 gift boxes, with 20 rupees left over.
Check the sharing. Bhavna has 4 parts, and 4 times 40 is 160. 200 plus 160 is 360, the whole amount, so the shares are right.
So the plan: count the parts, find one part, multiply for the share. And when you are buying whole things, leftover money that cannot buy one more is simply left over.
Riya and Karan share 360 rupees in the ratio of their ages. Riya spends her share on diyas that cost 12 rupees each. How many diyas can she buy?
Riya is 9 years old and Karan is 6. So the ratio of their ages, Riya to Karan, is 9 to 6.
Those numbers can be made simpler. What is the biggest number that divides both 9 and 6 exactly?

ask.ifNot: 9 is 3 times 3, and 6 is 2 times 3. Nothing bigger goes into both.

beats.say: 9 divided by 3 is 3, and 6 divided by 3 is 2. So 9 to 6 is the same ratio as 3 to 2, just in smaller numbers.
A ratio of 3 to 2 means equal parts: 3 parts for Riya and 2 parts for Karan. Here they are as boxes.
Before sharing anything, count. How many equal parts altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 3 and 2 make 5 parts.

beats.say: Add the ratio numbers: 3 plus 2 makes 5. All 360 rupees sit in those 5 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 360 divided by 5 is 72, so each part is 72 rupees. The classic slip is to divide by just one ratio number, but the total belongs to all 5 parts.
Riya has 3 parts, and each part is 72 rupees. 3 times 72 is 216, so Riya gets 216 rupees.
Each diya costs 12 rupees, so we need the number of 12s in 216. 12 times 10 is 120, and 12 times 8 is 96. Together that makes 216, so 12 goes in 18 times.
So Riya can buy 18 diyas.
Check the sharing. Karan has 2 parts, and 2 times 72 is 144. 216 plus 144 is 360, the whole amount, so the shares are right.
So remember three moves: count the parts, find one part, multiply for the share. Then do whatever else the story asks.
Ananya and Bhavya share a profit of 480 rupees in the ratio 3 to 5, the same as the money they put in. How much more does Bhavya get than Ananya?
Think of the ratio as equal boxes: 3 parts for Ananya and 5 parts for Bhavya.
Before sharing anything, count. How many equal parts altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 3 and 5 make 8 parts.

beats.say: 3 plus 5 is 8. So the 480 rupees are shared into 8 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 480 divided by 8 is 60, so each part is 60 rupees. The classic slip is to divide by just one ratio number, but the total belongs to all 8 parts.
Ananya has 3 parts: 3 times 60 is 180. Bhavya has 5 parts: 5 times 60 is 300.
The question asks how much more Bhavya gets than Ananya. What do we do with 300 and 180?

ask.ifNot: How much more asks for the gap between the two shares. To find a gap, take the smaller from the bigger: 300 minus 180.

beats.say: 300 minus 180 is 120. That gap is what the question wants.
So Bhavya receives 120 rupees more than Ananya.
Check it another way. Bhavya has 2 parts more than Ananya, and 2 times 60 is 120. The same answer, so we can trust it.
So remember three moves: count the parts, find one part, multiply for the share. Then do whatever else the story asks.
Riya buys 25 packets of gulal, pink to yellow in the ratio 3 to 2. A pink packet costs 15 rupees and a yellow packet costs 20 rupees. How much does she spend altogether?
Think of the ratio as equal boxes: 3 parts for pink and 2 parts for yellow.
First job: how many equal parts are there in all?

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 3 and 2 make 5 parts.

beats.say: 3 plus 2 is 5. So the 25 packets are shared into 5 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 25 divided by 5 is 5, so each part is 5 packets. Careful: we divide by all 5 parts, not by one of the ratio numbers on its own.
Pink has 3 parts: 3 times 5 is 15 packets. Yellow has 2 parts: 2 times 5 is 10 packets.
Now the money. There are 15 pink packets at 15 rupees each. Which sum gives their cost?

ask.ifNot: Each of the 15 pink packets costs 15 rupees. 15 lots of 15 is 15 times 15.

beats.say: 15 times 15 is 225 rupees for pink. And 10 yellow packets at 20 rupees each cost 10 times 20, which is 200 rupees.
Add the two costs: 225 plus 200 is 425.
So Riya spends 425 rupees altogether.
Check the sharing: 15 plus 10 is 25, the whole amount. The shares are right.
So the plan: use the ratio to find how many of each kind, multiply each kind by its own price, then add the two costs.
Riya and Sameer collect packets in the ratio 3 to 5. Sameer and Tina collect in the ratio 2 to 3. Tina collected 45 packets, and we want Riya's.
Notice that Sameer is in both ratios, and that makes a bridge between Riya and Tina. But careful: the parts in one ratio are not the same size as the parts in the other.
We know a real number for Tina. So which ratio do we start with?

ask.ifNot: Start where you know a real number. Tina is in the ratio Sameer to Tina, so we begin there.

beats.say: In that ratio Tina has 3 parts, and those are worth 45 packets. So one part is 45 divided by 3, which is 15.
Sameer has 2 of those parts. 2 times 15 is 30, so Sameer has 30 packets.
Now cross the bridge to the other ratio. There, Sameer has 5 parts, and we know Sameer has 30. What is one part this time?

ask.ifNot: In the ratio Riya to Sameer, the 30 belong to Sameer, who has 5 parts. So one part is 30 divided by 5.

beats.say: 30 divided by 5 is 6. See how these parts are a different size from the first ones? That is why we could not mix the two ratios.
Riya has 3 parts in this ratio. 3 times 6 is 18.
So Riya collected 18 packets.
Check both ratios. 18 to 30: divide both by 6 and you get 3 to 5. 30 to 45: divide both by 15 and you get 2 to 3.
So when one person sits in two ratios, use them as a bridge: find their real number from the ratio you know, then carry it into the other ratio.
Kabir and Riya collected money in the ratio 3 to 5. Riya and Sanya collected in the ratio 4 to 7. Kabir collected 1,800 rupees, and we want Sanya's amount.
Notice that Riya is in both ratios, and that makes a bridge between Kabir and Sanya. But careful: the parts in one ratio are not the same size as the parts in the other.
We know a real number for Kabir. So which ratio do we start with?

ask.ifNot: Start where you know a real number. Kabir is in the ratio Kabir to Riya, so we begin there.

beats.say: In that ratio Kabir has 3 parts, and those are worth 1,800 rupees. So one part is 1,800 divided by 3, which is 600.
Riya has 5 of those parts. 5 times 600 is 3,000, so Riya has 3,000 rupees.
Now cross the bridge to the other ratio. There, Riya has 4 parts, and we know Riya has 3,000. What is one part this time?

ask.ifNot: In the ratio Riya to Sanya, the 3,000 belong to Riya, who has 4 parts. So one part is 3,000 divided by 4.

beats.say: 3,000 divided by 4 is 750. See how these parts are a different size from the first ones? That is why we could not mix the two ratios.
Sanya has 7 parts in this ratio. 7 times 750 is 5,250.
So Sanya collected 5,250 rupees.
Check both ratios. 1,800 to 3,000: divide both by 600 and you get 3 to 5. 3,000 to 5,250: divide both by 750 and you get 4 to 7.
So when one person sits in two ratios, use them as a bridge: find their real number from the ratio you know, then carry it into the other ratio.
Kabir and Lakshmi collected money in the ratio 3 to 5. Lakshmi and Neha collected in the ratio 4 to 7. Kabir collected 360 rupees, and we want Neha's amount.
Notice that Lakshmi is in both ratios, and that makes a bridge between Kabir and Neha. But careful: the parts in one ratio are not the same size as the parts in the other.
We know a real number for Kabir. So which ratio do we start with?

ask.ifNot: Start where you know a real number. Kabir is in the ratio Kabir to Lakshmi, so we begin there.

beats.say: In that ratio Kabir has 3 parts, and those are worth 360 rupees. So one part is 360 divided by 3, which is 120.
Lakshmi has 5 of those parts. 5 times 120 is 600, so Lakshmi has 600 rupees.
Now cross the bridge to the other ratio. There, Lakshmi has 4 parts, and we know Lakshmi has 600. What is one part this time?

ask.ifNot: In the ratio Lakshmi to Neha, the 600 belong to Lakshmi, who has 4 parts. So one part is 600 divided by 4.

beats.say: 600 divided by 4 is 150. See how these parts are a different size from the first ones? That is why we could not mix the two ratios.
Neha has 7 parts in this ratio. 7 times 150 is 1,050.
So Neha collected 1,050 rupees.
Check both ratios. 360 to 600: divide both by 120 and you get 3 to 5. 600 to 1,050: divide both by 150 and you get 4 to 7.
So when one person sits in two ratios, use them as a bridge: find their real number from the ratio you know, then carry it into the other ratio.
Rohit's and Virat's runs were in the ratio 5 to 3. Then Rohit scored 18 more and Virat scored 42 more, and their totals became equal. We want Rohit's total over both matches.
We don't know the runs yet, only the parts. In the first match Rohit has 5 equal parts and Virat has 3. Each bar then gets its extra runs.

spec.note: After both matches the two bars are equal

beats.say: After the second match the totals are equal. So 5 parts plus 18 is the same as 3 parts plus 42.
Both sides have at least 3 parts. If we take 3 parts off each side, what is left?

ask.ifNot: Taking the same thing from both sides keeps them equal. 5 parts take away 3 parts leaves 2 parts on the left, and the 42 stays alone on the right.

beats.say: So 2 parts plus 18 equals 42.
Now take the 18 away from both sides. 42 minus 18 is 24, so 2 parts are worth 24 runs.
If 2 parts are 24 runs, one part is 24 divided by 2, which is 12.
Rohit had 5 parts in the first match. Which sum gives his runs in that match?

ask.ifNot: Each part is 12 runs, and Rohit has 5 of them. 5 lots of 12 is 5 times 12.

beats.say: 5 times 12 is 60. But careful: the question wants his runs across both matches, so we add the 18. 60 plus 18 is 78.
So Rohit scored 78 runs across both matches.
Check with Virat. 3 times 12 is 36, and 36 plus 42 is 78 as well. The totals are equal, just as the story says.
So when a ratio hides the real numbers, work in parts: write what the story says using parts, find one part, then go back for what the question asks.
Red and yellow paint are mixed in the ratio 3 to 5, and 24 litres of yellow paint were used. We want the litres of red.
The ratio means equal parts: 3 parts of red for every 5 parts of yellow.
Here is the trap in this question. What is the 24 litres?

ask.ifNot: Read it once more: they used 24 litres of yellow paint. So 24 is not the total. It is the yellow on its own.

beats.say: So this time we do not add 3 and 5. The 24 litres fill yellow's 5 parts, and nothing else.
One part is 24 divided by 5. A neat way to divide by 5 is to double, then divide by 10. Double 24 is 48, and 48 divided by 10 is 4.8.
So each part is 4.8 litres. Red has 3 parts. Which sum gives the red paint?

ask.ifNot: Each part is 4.8 litres, and red has 3 parts. So we want 3 lots of 4.8.

beats.say: 3 times 4 is 12, and 3 times 0.8 is 2.4. Add them: 12 plus 2.4 is 14.4.
So they used 14.4 litres of red paint.
Check: red has fewer parts than yellow, and 14.4 is less than 24, so that fits. And 5 parts of 4.8 give back the 24 litres of yellow.
So before you share in a ratio, ask what the number in the story belongs to. If it is one share, divide by that share's parts, not by all the parts.
In Lakshmi's triangle the largest angle is three times the smallest, and the middle angle is 20 degrees more than the smallest. We want the type of triangle.
Everything is described using the smallest angle, so let's call that one x. Then the middle angle is x plus 20, and the largest is 3 x.

spec.note: The three angles together make the whole triangle

beats.say: Before we go on: what do the three angles of any triangle add up to?

ask.ifNot: A square corner is 90 degrees and a full turn is 360. The three angles of a triangle always make a half turn, a straight line, which is 180 degrees.

beats.say: So our three angles together make 180: x, plus x plus 20, plus 3 x.

board.text: Angles of a triangle add up to 180°

beats.say: Count the x's: 1 and 1 and 3 make 5 x. So 5 x plus 20 equals 180.
To undo plus 20, we take 20 from both sides. 180 minus 20 is 160, so 5 x is 160.
5 x means 5 times x, so we divide both sides by 5. 160 divided by 5 is 32, so x is 32 degrees.
The type of a triangle is decided by its largest angle, and that is 3 x. 3 times 32 is 96 degrees.
The largest angle is 96 degrees, and a right angle is 90 degrees. So what kind of triangle is this?

ask.ifNot: Compare 96 with 90. It is more than a right angle, and a triangle with an angle bigger than a right angle is called obtuse-angled.

beats.say: One angle bigger than 90 degrees makes the whole triangle obtuse-angled. For the record, the middle angle is 32 plus 20, which is 52 degrees.
So Lakshmi has drawn an obtuse-angled triangle.
Check: 32 plus 52 plus 96 is 180. The three angles fit a triangle.
So the method: call the smallest angle x, write every angle using x, make them add up to 180, and solve. Then let the largest angle name the triangle.
In Deepa's tile, one angle is twice the smallest angle, and the largest is three times the smallest. We want the largest angle.
Everything is measured against the smallest angle, so let's call that one x. Then the other two angles are 2 x and 3 x.

spec.note: The three angles together make the whole triangle

beats.say: Before we go on: what do the three angles of any triangle add up to?

ask.ifNot: A square corner is 90 degrees and a full turn is 360. The three angles of a triangle always make a half turn, a straight line, which is 180 degrees.

beats.say: So our three angles together make 180: x, plus 2 x, plus 3 x.

board.text: Angles of a triangle add up to 180°

beats.say: Count the x's: 1 and 2 and 3 make 6 x. So 6 x equals 180.
6 x means 6 times x, so we divide both sides by 6. 180 divided by 6 is 30, so x is 30 degrees.
Careful, x is the smallest angle, and the question wants the largest. Which sum gives the largest angle?

ask.ifNot: The largest angle is three times the smallest, and the smallest is 30. So we want 3 times 30.

beats.say: 3 times 30 is 90. And the angle in the middle is 2 times 30, which is 60.
So the largest angle is 90 degrees, a right angle. Deepa's tile is a right-angled triangle.
Check: 30 plus 60 plus 90 is 180. The three angles fit a triangle.
So the method: call the unknown angle x, write every angle using x, make them add up to 180, and solve. Then read the question again to see what it really wants.
In Meera's banner, the first angle is 15 degrees more than the second, and the third is 25 degrees more than the second. We want the type of triangle.
Both clues lean on the second angle, so let's call it x. Then the first angle is x plus 15, and the third is x plus 25.

spec.note: The three angles together make the whole triangle

beats.say: Before we go on: what do the three angles of any triangle add up to?

ask.ifNot: A square corner is 90 degrees and a full turn is 360. The three angles of a triangle always make a half turn, a straight line, which is 180 degrees.

beats.say: So our three angles together make 180: x plus 15, plus x, plus x plus 25.

board.text: Angles of a triangle add up to 180°

beats.say: There are 3 x's, and 15 plus 25 is 40. So 3 x plus 40 equals 180. Take 40 from both sides, and 3 x equals 140.
Now, 140 does not divide by 3 exactly. 3 times 46 is 138 and 3 times 47 is 141, so x is somewhere between 46 and 47 degrees.
That is fine, because we only need the type of triangle. Which angle decides the type?

ask.ifNot: If the largest angle is under a right angle, the other two must be as well. So the largest one, x plus 25, decides the type.

beats.say: x is less than 47, so the largest angle is less than 47 plus 25, which is 72.
72 is well under 90, the size of a right angle. So all three angles are smaller than a right angle.
A triangle whose angles are all less than 90 degrees is an acute-angled triangle. That is Meera's banner.
Check another way. If the largest angle were 90, the second would be 65 and the first 80. Those add up to 235, far more than 180, so the real angles must be smaller.
So the method: write every angle using x and make them add up to 180. And when you only need the type, you just need to know which side of 90 the largest angle falls.
Sanya's flag is a triangle with exactly two equal sides, and the angle between those two sides is 40 degrees. We want each of the other two angles.

board.text: Two equal sides, angle between them = 40°

beats.say: A triangle with two equal sides is called isosceles. Its special trick: the two angles opposite the equal sides are equal to each other.

board.text: The other two angles are equal

beats.say: Before we go on: what do the three angles of any triangle add up to?

ask.ifNot: Tear the three corners off a paper triangle and put them side by side. They always make a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees.

beats.say: So the 40 and the two equal angles make 180. Take the 40 away: 180 minus 40 is 140.

board.text: Angles of a triangle add up to 180°

beats.say: That 140 is for both of the equal angles together. So how big is each one?

ask.ifNot: The 140 is shared by two angles of the same size. Sharing equally between 2 means dividing by 2.

beats.say: 140 divided by 2 is 70. Careful: this is where many people stop at 140, but that is two angles, not one.
So each of the other two angles is 70 degrees.
Check: 40 plus 70 plus 70 is 180. It fits.
So for a triangle with two equal sides: take the angle between them from 180, then halve what is left.
The three angles of Farhan's garden are in the ratio 3 to 5 to 7. We must find the largest angle and name the triangle. The 12 metre side is extra: only the angles matter here.
One fact unlocks this. What do the three angles of any triangle add up to?

ask.ifNot: A square corner is 90 degrees and a full turn is 360. The three angles of a triangle always make a half turn, a straight line, which is 180 degrees.

beats.say: So 180 degrees is shared between the three angles in the ratio 3 to 5 to 7. Count the parts: 3 plus 5 plus 7 is 15.

board.text: Angles of a triangle add up to 180°

beats.say: 15 equal parts make 180 degrees. So one part is 180 divided by 15, which is 12 degrees.
Now each angle. 3 times 12 is 36, 5 times 12 is 60, and 7 times 12 is 84.
To name the triangle, compare the largest angle, 84 degrees, with a right angle, 90 degrees. What kind of triangle is it?

ask.ifNot: 84 is less than 90, so even the largest angle is smaller than a right angle. A triangle like that is acute-angled.

beats.say: Don't be fooled because 84 is close to 90. It is still less, so all three angles are acute, and the triangle is acute-angled.
So it is an acute-angled triangle, and its largest angle is 84 degrees.
Check: 36 plus 60 plus 84 is 180. The three angles fit a triangle.
So for angles in a ratio: share 180 degrees into the parts, find each angle, then let the largest angle name the triangle.
Tanvi's flag is an isosceles triangle with 40 degrees between its two equal sides. Then she changes that angle to 100 degrees. We want the difference between the base angles, new and old.
In an isosceles triangle, the two base angles, the ones opposite the equal sides, are equal to each other.

board.text: The two base angles are equal

beats.say: Before we go on: what do the three angles of any triangle add up to?

ask.ifNot: A square corner is 90 degrees and a full turn is 360. The three angles of a triangle always make a half turn, a straight line, which is 180 degrees.

beats.say: Start with the first triangle. Take the 40 away from 180, and 140 is left for the two base angles together.

board.text: Angles of a triangle add up to 180°

beats.say: Those two base angles are equal. So how big is each one?

ask.ifNot: The 140 is shared by two angles of the same size. Sharing equally between 2 means dividing by 2.

beats.say: 140 divided by 2 is 70. So each base angle of the first triangle is 70 degrees.
Now the new triangle, done the very same way. 180 minus 100 is 80, and 80 divided by 2 is 40. Each base angle is now 40 degrees.
The question asks for the difference, so compare one base angle from each triangle. 70 minus 40 is 30.
So each base angle is 30 degrees smaller in the new triangle.
Check both triangles. 40 plus 70 plus 70 is 180, and 100 plus 40 plus 40 is 180. Both fit.
So for any isosceles triangle: take the angle between the equal sides from 180, then halve what is left to get each base angle.
Arjun's bamboo triangle has one angle of 90 degrees and another of 35 degrees. We want the third angle.
Here is the fact we need. What do the three angles of a triangle always add up to?

ask.ifNot: Tear the three corners off a paper triangle and put them side by side. They always make a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees.

beats.say: Add the two angles we know. 90 plus 35 is 125.

board.text: Angles of a triangle add up to 180°

beats.say: The three angles must make 180, and the ones we know use up 125. How do we find the third?

ask.ifNot: The third angle is whatever is left of the 180 once the other two are taken out. Finding what is left is a take away. So it is 180 minus 125.

beats.say: 180 minus 125 is 55. Careful not to stop at 125: that is the two angles we already had, not the missing one.
So the third angle of Arjun's triangle is 55 degrees.
Check: 90 plus 35 plus 55 is 180. And here is a bonus: in a right-angled triangle the other two angles always make 90, and 35 plus 55 is 90.
So to find the third angle of any triangle: add the two you know, and take the total from 180.
Neha's bookmark has two angles of 70 degrees each. She says it is both an acute triangle and an isosceles triangle. We must find the third angle and decide if she is right.
Before we go on: what do the three angles of any triangle add up to?

ask.ifNot: Tear the three corners off a paper triangle and put them side by side. They always make a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees.

beats.say: 70 plus 70 is 140, and 180 minus 140 leaves 40. So the third angle is 40 degrees.

board.text: Angles of a triangle add up to 180°

beats.say: Now test Neha's word isosceles. A triangle is isosceles when two of its angles are equal. Here two angles are both 70, so yes.
Now her other word, acute. What must be true for a triangle to be acute?

ask.ifNot: Every triangle has some angles under 90 degrees, so one is not enough. A triangle is acute only when all three of its angles are less than 90 degrees.

beats.say: Look at each one: 70, 70 and 40 are all less than 90. So it is acute as well.
So Neha is correct on both counts, and the third angle is 40 degrees.
Check: 70 plus 70 plus 40 is 180. It fits.
So find the missing angle from 180 first. Then test each name on its own: equal angles for isosceles, all angles under 90 for acute.
Kavya's triangle has an angle of 60 degrees, and the two sides that form it are both 7 centimetres. We want each of the other two angles.

board.text: One angle = 60°, between two sides of 7 cm

beats.say: Two equal sides make this an isosceles triangle. So the two angles opposite those sides, the ones we want, are equal to each other.

board.text: The other two angles are equal

beats.say: Here is the fact we need. What do the three angles of a triangle always add up to?

ask.ifNot: A square corner is 90 degrees and a full turn is 360. The three angles of a triangle always make a half turn, a straight line, which is 180 degrees.

beats.say: Take the 60 away from 180. That leaves 120 for the other two angles together.

board.text: Angles of a triangle add up to 180°

beats.say: That 120 is for both angles together, and they are equal. So how big is each one?

ask.ifNot: The 120 is shared by two angles of the same size. Sharing equally between 2 means dividing by 2.

beats.say: 120 divided by 2 is 60. Careful not to stop at 120: that is both angles together.
So each of the other two angles is 60 degrees.
Look what happened: all three angles are 60 degrees, and 60 plus 60 plus 60 is 180. So this triangle is equilateral, and its third side is 7 centimetres too.
So for a triangle with two equal sides: take the angle between them from 180, then halve what is left.
Rohan's window frame has sides of 6, 8 and 10 centimetres. He notices that the longest side squared equals the squares of the other two sides added together. We want the type of triangle.
Let's test what Rohan noticed for ourselves. First, what does 6 squared mean?

ask.ifNot: Squared means a number times itself. So 6 squared is 6 times 6, not 6 times 2.

beats.say: 6 squared is 6 times 6, which is 36. And 8 squared is 8 times 8, which is 64.
Add those two squares: 36 plus 64 is 100.
Now the longest side. 10 squared is 10 times 10, and that is 100 as well. The two results match, so Rohan is right.
Only one kind of triangle has sides that do this. Which kind?

ask.ifNot: This is the special rule of right-angled triangles, named after Pythagoras. When the squares match like this, the angle opposite the longest side is a right angle.

beats.say: It is the rule of Pythagoras. The squares match exactly only when the triangle has a right angle, and that angle sits opposite the longest side.
So the window frame is a right-angled triangle.
Check the other names. It cannot be equilateral, because its three sides are all different. And the matching squares rule out acute and obtuse.
So to test for a right angle using only the sides: square the two shorter sides, add them, and see whether you get the longest side squared.
